beads.title: Stop sending UDP when control puts this node in TCP-443-only mode
beads.description: Control's only way to tell a client "this network alarms on anything that is not TCP 443" does nothing to this node. At commit 023255e8a27ec9f6a21d24e3eda21c052ff72af3, tailcfg/nodecap/nodecap.go documents OnlyTCP443 ("only-tcp-443") as meaning the client "should not attempt to generate any outbound traffic that isn't TCP on port 443", which "thus implies all traffic is over DERP". Go reads the attribute off the SELF node in ipn/ipnlocal/local.go:2064 and calls MagicConn().SetOnlyTCP443 (wgengine/magicsock/derp.go:791), and the flag then gates four things. magicsock.sendUDPStd -- the single chokepoint every UDP send in magicsock passes through, disco and WireGuard data alike -- returns (false, nil): not an error, a SILENT refusal, which is precisely what makes the caller fall back to DERP rather than mark the path broken. sendUDPNetcheck returns errors.ErrUnsupported, so netcheck's STUN probes stop rather than record a failure. netcheck skips makeProbePlan entirely (net/netcheck/netcheck.go:940) and skips the ICMP latency probes (:1008), so the report is built from HTTPS measurements only. The endpoint-update path's noV4Send re-bind is suppressed (magicsock.go:921) and the portmapper is disabled wholesale (feature/portmapper's DisableAll). This repository implements none of it: the string only-tcp-443 appears nowhere in the workspace, and ts_magicsock::MagicSock writes UDP from its one bound socket with no gate above it -- send_stun_request (ts_magicsock/src/sock.rs:1933) emits Binding Requests on a 20-26s cadence, send_pings emits disco, send_wireguard emits data. So a node an operator deployed into a locked-down network, and which control has explicitly asked to go quiet, keeps emitting UDP to STUN servers, to peers and to relay servers -- which is the outbound-firewall alarm the attribute exists to prevent. Unusually for a parity gap the cost lands on the deployer's own network rather than on the tailnet. The port is well shaped for this fork because the refusal is a chokepoint and this fork already builds chokepoints: the capability map already reaches the domain node as ts_control::Node::cap_map and is already queried by Node::has_node_attr (that is how cache-network-maps is honoured today), so the work is one read of the self node's attributes, one flag on MagicSock, and one early return in the single place the socket is written. Carry Go's refusal KINDS exactly, because they differ on purpose: the data path's silent false engages the DERP fallback, while netcheck's explicit ErrUnsupported marks a probe skipped rather than failed. Collapsing them into one refusal either marks every peer unreachable or fabricates a netcheck result. Test the negatives: DERP traffic is unaffected; a refused send is not logged as a send error; a netcheck run under the attribute produces a report with no STUN and no ICMP rather than an empty or invalid one; and clearing the attribute restores UDP without a restart, because Go's SetOnlyTCP443 is live rather than start-time. Scope: this bead is closed by the UDP-send and netcheck gates above, honoured live. only-tcp-443 ALSO disables the peer-relay client, and that half belongs to the disable-relay-client bead because it is the same Go predicate read at the same place; whichever of the two lands first should introduce the shared predicate, and this bead is not held open waiting for the other. The portmapper arm is not in scope at all: there is no portmapper here to disable. See PORTING.md section B.

beads.title: Honour disable-relay-client instead of opening relay paths control switched off
beads.description: This node will keep using peer-relay paths after control has told it to stop. At commit 023255e8a27ec9f6a21d24e3eda21c052ff72af3, wgengine/magicsock/magicsock.go:3000 computes relayClientEnabled := self.Valid() && !self.HasCap(nodecap.DisableRelayClient) && !self.HasCap(nodecap.OnlyTCP443) once per netmap, and gates three behaviours on it. An inbound CallMeMaybeVia from a peer is DROPPED (magicsock.go:2331, "ignoring %s from %v; disable-relay-client node attr is set") -- silently as far as the peer is concerned, with only a local log. The relay-server set is cleared rather than recomputed (magicsock.go:3050 calls relayManager.handleRelayServersSet(nil)). And SetFilter returns early (magicsock.go:2858) instead of re-deriving the relay server set from the new filter. nodecap.go documents the attribute as dynamically settable: adding it to a running node stops new allocations and new paths at its next network map, and deliberately does NOT tear down paths already in use. This repository has the relay client half and no gate on it. ts_magicsock's relay module implements the CallMeMaybeVia to 3-way bind handshake to relayed ping/pong path (ts_magicsock/src/relay.rs), and the ingress arm at ts_magicsock/src/sock.rs:1203 admits a CallMeMaybeVia on call_me_maybe_sender_allowed alone -- a peer-identity check with no node-attribute check beside it -- then calls start_relay_handshake. The strings disable-relay-client and only-tcp-443 appear nowhere in the workspace. So control can tell this node to stop being a relay client and it will go on handshaking with relay servers and opening relayed paths, which is both a divergence a control plane can observe and traffic a deployer did not ask for. The work is small and lands in one place: call_me_maybe_sender_allowed is already the right chokepoint and already carries the metric for the refusal (disco_call_me_maybe_via_recv_rejected), and the capability map already reaches the tree as ts_control::Node::cap_map with Node::has_node_attr to query it. Carry Go's two bounds exactly, because they are the behaviour rather than decoration: the drop is silent to the peer (no disco reply of any kind, just a log), and an existing relayed path is NOT torn down when the attribute appears -- only new ones are refused, so a test must assert that an already-established relay path keeps carrying traffic. Implement the predicate as Go writes it, with both attributes in it, so that whichever of this and the only-tcp-443 bead lands second does not introduce a second, divergent read. See PORTING.md section B.

beads.title: Suppress disco heartbeats when control sets silent-disco
beads.description: A peer that a Go client would have stopped pinging still gets a disco ping from this node every two seconds. At commit 023255e8a27ec9f6a21d24e3eda21c052ff72af3, the silent-disco node attribute reaches magicsock through controlknobs (control/controlknobs/controlknobs.go, SilentDisco) and ipn/ipnlocal/local.go:7369 (b.MagicConn().SetSilentDisco(...)), is folded with the TS_DEBUG_ENABLE_SILENT_DISCO envknob in debugFlagsLocked (wgengine/magicsock/magicsock.go:2802), and is pushed onto every endpoint as heartbeatDisabled (endpoint.go:1694). Three sites read it. noteTxActivityExtTriggerLocked (endpoint.go:1016) does not arm the heartBeatTimer at all, so the 3s re-ping is never scheduled. heartbeat (endpoint.go:879) returns immediately when it fires with the flag set. And -- the compensating half, which is the part a port forgets -- noteRecvActivity's else arm (endpoint.go:591) extends trustBestAddrUntil directly when an inbound packet arrives from the current best address, because with no heartbeat there is nothing else keeping that path trusted. Upstream's own comment there marks the arm as provisional ("subject to change as part of silent disco effort"), which is a reason to port it verbatim rather than to improve on it. This repository's equivalent machinery is ts_magicsock's path table plus the global pinger: the confirmed best path is re-pinged every PING_INTERVAL (2s, ts_runtime/src/direct.rs:106) and is explicitly exempt from the DISCO_PING_INTERVAL floor that throttles other candidates (ts_magicsock/src/path.rs:428). path.rs documents the relationship to Go's heartbeatInterval in detail and nowhere mentions that control can switch the whole thing off; the string silent-disco appears nowhere in the workspace. The result is peer-observable and at a tighter cadence than Go's. The work is the flag plus its compensating arm, and the second is not optional: suppressing the re-ping without extending trust on inbound data lets TRUST_DURATION lapse on a path that is demonstrably alive and demotes a working direct peer to DERP -- a regression strictly worse than the gap. The capability map already reaches the tree as ts_control::Node::cap_map with Node::has_node_attr, and the attribute is read from the SELF node, not from the peer. Assert both: with the attribute set and data flowing, no disco ping is emitted to that peer AND the best path stays trusted rather than falling back to DERP; with the attribute absent, the existing 2s cadence is unchanged. See PORTING.md section B.

beads.title: Stop the periodic STUN sweep when the datapath goes idle
beads.description: This node emits STUN Binding Requests every 20-26 seconds for its entire life; a real tailscaled goes quiet 45 seconds after the last packet. At commit 023255e8a27ec9f6a21d24e3eda21c052ff72af3, wgengine/magicsock/magicsock.go:3607, shouldDoPeriodicReSTUNLocked, has four stop conditions: the network being down or the node homeless; having no peers or no private key; and -- the one this bead is about -- the datapath having been idle longer than sessionActiveTimeout (45s, magicsock.go:3990), measured through the idleFunc that wgengine/userspace.go:435 wires to the TUN device's IdleDuration. That last arm has exactly one override: if control set debug-always-stun (controlknobs.ForceBackgroundSTUN), the sweep keeps running regardless. This repository ports one of the four and says so. ts_runtime::direct::stun_probe_should_run (ts_runtime/src/direct.rs:718) returns true whenever a netmap with at least one peer is loaded, and its doc comment records that Go's other three "need activity/network-state plumbing the runtime does not have yet". That is an honest note in the code that has never been an entry in the parity ledger, which is what this bead closes. The behavioural consequence is the one that same doc comment gives as the reason for porting the peer-count arm, now applied to the arm that was not ported: a node with peers and no traffic keeps STUNning the DERP map's STUN servers forever, and "steady STUN with no peer traffic" is exactly the fingerprint the peer-count arm exists to avoid. Scope, so this is neither over- nor under-built: this bead is closed by the idle arm plus its debug-always-stun override, and by nothing else. The zero-private-key arm is structurally impossible here -- the socket is bound with a real key before run_stun_prober is spawned -- so record it in a comment rather than implement it, and that record closes it. The network-down and homeless arms need a ts_netmon OS backend that does not exist; they are deliberately excluded and should be cut as their own bead when that backend lands, not folded into this one. The idle arm needs one timestamp, the last datapath send, and both the TUN and netstack paths already flow through a point where it can be recorded. Port debug-always-stun in the same commit and at the same place Go puts it: the attribute means nothing until there is an idle arm to override, and adding the idle stop without the override would take away control's only way to ask for today's behaviour. The capability map already reaches the tree as ts_control::Node::cap_map with Node::has_node_attr. Assert both directions -- idle past the timeout stops the sweep, and idle past the timeout WITH the attribute does not -- plus the negative that matters for connectivity: traffic resuming re-starts the sweep without waiting for a netmap change. See PORTING.md section B.

beads.title: Fall back to full netmap rebuilds when control sets disable-delta-updates
beads.description: Control has an escape hatch for a delta-encoding bug on either side of the map protocol, and this node ignores it. At commit 023255e8a27ec9f6a21d24e3eda21c052ff72af3, the first statement in control/controlclient/map.go's tryHandleIncrementally (map.go:349) is "if ms.controlKnobs != nil && ms.controlKnobs.DisableDeltaUpdates.Load() { return false }", and returning false is what makes the map session fall back to rebuilding the whole netmap from the response instead of applying it as mutations. The knob is filled from the disable-delta-updates node attribute (control/controlknobs/controlknobs.go, DisableDeltaUpdates), whose own documentation states the intent: it makes the client "not process updates via the delta update mechanism and should instead treat all netmap changes as 'full' ones as tailscaled did in 1.48.x and earlier". It exists so control can switch a client off the incremental path without shipping a client release. This repository implements the delta path and has no escape hatch. ts_control's map stream applies MapResponse.PeersChangedPatch after the whole-node Peers* set, in Go's order, with the ordering rationale written out (ts_control/src/tokio/map_stream.rs:382), and the string disable-delta-updates appears nowhere in the workspace. So if control needs this node to stop trusting patches -- because control is emitting bad ones, or because this client is applying them wrongly -- there is no way to say so, and this node's view of the tailnet can stay wrong for as long as the map session lasts, which for a long poll is indefinitely. The work is the early return plus the fall-back-to-full behaviour, at the one place the patch set is applied, with the attribute read from the self node through the capability map that already reaches the tree as ts_control::Node::cap_map (Node::has_node_attr). The refusal to carry is Go's exact shape and it is easy to get wrong: the attribute does not REJECT the response and does not drop the patches, it declines the incremental path so that the full path handles the same response. A response carrying only PeersChangedPatch must therefore still be applied under the attribute -- as a full update -- and a test that asserts such a response is ignored would be pinning the wrong behaviour. Assert the positive too: with the attribute absent the patch path is unchanged, including the Peers*-then-patch ordering the module documents. See PORTING.md section B.

beads.title: Retry a truncated upstream DNS answer over TCP instead of returning it truncated
beads.description: A DNS name whose answer does not fit a datagram is unresolvable through this node's forwarder, and the client's RFC-mandated retry has nowhere to go. At commit 023255e8a27ec9f6a21d24e3eda21c052ff72af3, net/dns/resolver/forwarder.go sends a forwarded query over UDP in its firstUDP closure, checks the TC (truncated) bit on the reply, and re-sends the same query to the SAME resolver over TCP when it is set, logging which way the retry went. forwarder.go:677 is the switch: skipTCP := skipTCPRetry() || (f.controlKnobs != nil && f.controlKnobs.DisableDNSForwarderTCPRetries.Load()), where the knob comes from the dns-forwarder-disable-tcp-retries node attribute. The retry is ON by default and the attribute is its off switch; upstream dates the client's understanding of it to capability version 75 (2023-09-12). This repository does the client-facing half of truncation carefully and the upstream-facing half not at all. check_response_size_and_set_tc sizes a forwarded reply against the client's advertised EDNS limit and sets TC (ts_runtime/src/magic_dns.rs), and ts_runtime::dns_over_tcp serves the retry the stub resolver then makes over TCP to 100.100.100.100:53 -- where upstream Go would have answered with a RST -- so the retry path exists. But the hop to the upstream resolver is UDP on BOTH transports: forward_query calls ask_upstream (ts_runtime/src/magic_dns.rs:1115), which does a udp_bind on the overlay channel and nothing else, and the module's own comment already notes that "the hop to the *upstream* resolver is still UDP". The failure is concrete: an answer larger than MAX_UPSTREAM_RESPONSE (4095 bytes) -- a large DNSSEC set, a big TXT record set, a wide round-robin -- is truncated by the upstream hop, the client dutifully retries over TCP as RFC 1035 s4.2.1 requires, the TCP server forwards through the same UDP hop, and the same truncated answer comes back. The name resolves for a Go client and does not resolve here. The work is a TCP fallback inside ask_upstream, triggered on the TC bit of the UDP reply, carried over the SAME overlay netstack channel the UDP hop uses -- never a host socket. That coupling is this module's anti-leak property and must not be relaxed to make a TCP upstream easier to write. Then port dns-forwarder-disable-tcp-retries as the switch that turns the new retry back off, read from the self node through ts_control::Node::cap_map / Node::has_node_attr, which is the only reason control has to care about any of this. Carry Go's bounds, because they are where the leaks and the regressions are: the retry goes to the SAME resolver rather than the next one in the list (walking the list would send the query to a resolver the first one already answered); a TCP failure falls back to returning the truncated UDP answer rather than SERVFAIL; and a reply without TC set is never retried. See PORTING.md section B.

beads.title: Collapse host CGNAT routes on control's one-cgnat attribute, and above Go's threshold
beads.description: This node installs one host route per peer with no ceiling, and control's tri-state switch over that choice does nothing. At commit 023255e8a27ec9f6a21d24e3eda21c052ff72af3, net/routemanager/routemanager.go keeps the OS route set as one /32 per peer until the number of distinct CGNAT self-address routes exceeds cgnatThreshold (10000, routemanager.go:148), above which they collapse into the single 100.64.0.0/10. RouteManager.cgnatThreshold (routemanager.go:887) returns 1 instead of that constant when TailnetConfig.OneCGNAT is set, i.e. always collapse. The value is fed from control in ipn/ipnlocal/local.go: the one-cgnat node attributes are read into controlknobs.OneCGNAT as an opt.Bool (local.go:6210) and reach the route manager through node_backend.go:959's SetTailnetConfig. The tri-state is deliberate and is modelled as opt.Bool rather than bool for exactly that reason: nodecap.OneCGNATEnable ("one-cgnat?v=true") forces the collapsed route, nodecap.OneCGNATDisable ("one-cgnat?v=false") forces /32-per-peer, and neither present leaves the threshold to decide. This repository installs one /32 per peer unconditionally. ts_runtime::tun_actor::host_routes_from_node (ts_runtime/src/tun_actor.rs) folds every peer's routes_to_install into HostRoutes.routed with no collapse and no threshold, and neither one-cgnat?v=true nor one-cgnat?v=false appears anywhere in the workspace. Below 10000 peers that matches Go's default, which is why this is narrow rather than urgent; above it, or whenever control asks, it does not, and the automatic threshold exists precisely because a host route table with one entry per peer does not scale. Two notes for whoever picks this up. First, port the tri-state, not a boolean: an absent attribute must keep the threshold behaviour rather than defaulting either way, and ?v=false must force per-peer routes even above the threshold. Second, this is one of four upstream attributes whose key carries a query string, and that is why the parity ledger's node-attribute walk never reported it for six revisions -- its character class did not match ? or =. The capability map already reaches the tree as ts_control::Node::cap_map with Node::has_node_attr, so the lookup is by the full literal key including the query string. The negative to assert is the one that costs connectivity if it is wrong: the self /32 and the MagicDNS 100.100.100.100/32 are never folded into the /10, because they are routed-to-self and host_routes_from_node's existing push_v4 dedup depends on them staying distinct. Assert also that collapsing does not drop a peer's advertised subnet routes, which are not CGNAT prefixes and are not part of the collapse. This is host-OS-facing: no peer and no control plane observes the route table directly. Read it beside PORTING.md section A row 133, which is the other open host-OS-facing row. See PORTING.md section B.
